thread.title: Apple’s Plans Expose Big Misunderstandings About Corporate Repatriation

author: John Kimelman
title: Apple’s Plans Expose Big Misunderstandings About Corporate Repatriation
text:
Apple ( AAPL ) made big headlines Wednesday when it announced that it would pay about $38 billion in taxes on profits held abroad and spend $30 billion on a five-year investment program in the U.S., including a new corporate campus outside of the Bay Area.
In an interview with ABC News, Apple CEO Tim Cook cited the new tax law sharply lowering on tax on foreign profits as the reason for its $38 billion payment. But according to the Wall Street Journal , he didn't say how much of more than $250 billion in overseas cash holdings the company plans to bring home, though it should be the vast majority.
The Apple news is the biggest single corporate response thus far to a provision in the new tax bill dealing with the so-called "repatriation" of foreign profits. The news also exposes a few misunderstandings that many have about the new tax law's impact on foreign profits held by U.S. corporations.
Thankfully, Dan Clifton, a Washington-based policy analyst with Strategas Partners , has been immersed in the dry details of the tax bill for months. In a memo to clients Thursday, he dealt with a few misunderstandings that many members of the financial media seem to have with the legislation.
Let's start with the issue of which foreign profits are actually taxed under the new 15.5 % rate on cash and other liquid assets, and an 8% rate for illiquid assets.
Writes Clifton, "Congress imposed a mandatory tax on all unremitted foreign earnings overseas regardless of whether the money is repatriated back to the US." He added that companies have eight years to pay this tax off.
That should explain why Apple can know exactly how much its tax burden will be—$38 billion—even if the company isn't sure yet how much of its foreign profits it will bring back to the U.S.
Clifton also wants to clear up another misunderstanding which he thinks has taken on mythical status: the idea that almost all the foreign profits repatriated during the last U.S. "tax holiday" in 2005 went directly to shareholders in the form of dividends and share buybacks.
"No discussion about repatriation gets my blood boiling more than the quip that nearly all of the money from the 2005 repatriation tax holiday was used for share repurchases and dividends," writes Clifton. "This is based on an 'academic' study which severely misrepresents what happened in 2005."
Clifton writes that during the last repatriation tax holiday, companies voluntarily returned $300 billion of cash back to the US. And share repurchases in total for 2005 were $150 billion.
"Even if every share repurchase was from repatriation (which is an absurd starting point), you get 50%" he writes. "More than $30 billion of that was from a special Microsoft ( MSFT ) share repurchase announced the previous year, long before repatriation was even a legislative possibility. It’s nearly impossible to make the math work that 90% was used for share repurchases and dividends."
If Clifton is on the mark, it might mean that the U.S. economy could get a bigger boost than previously thought and shareholders might not get as large a gift as they expected.
